content.page_title: Generic Semaglutide for Weight Loss in Canada (2026): Off-Label Guide
content.meta_description: Generic semaglutide is now available in Canada from $114/month. Can you use it for weight loss? Yes — off-label. Here's what to tell your doctor, which telehealth providers prescribe it, and what to expect.
content.h1: Generic Semaglutide for Weight Loss in Canada: The Complete Guide
content.quick_summary: Generic semaglutide (Apo-Semaglutide, Dr. Reddy's) is approved for Type 2 diabetes in Canada — but doctors can legally prescribe it off-label for weight loss, exactly as they do with brand-name Ozempic. At $114/month vs. $250–500 for Ozempic, the generic makes medically supervised weight loss significantly more affordable for Canadians.
content.intro: Generic semaglutide changed the math on GLP-1 weight loss treatment in Canada. What was a $250–500/month expense is now available from $114/month — and the drug is clinically identical to Ozempic. But there's a catch most articles skip over: the 2026 generics are approved for Type 2 diabetes, not weight loss. That doesn't mean you can't use them for weight loss — it means you need a specific type of prescription from a doctor willing to prescribe off-label. This guide explains exactly how that works and what your options are.

body_sections.heading: What 'Off-Label' Means — and Why It's Completely Legal
body_sections.body: When Health Canada approves a drug, it approves it for specific indications (medical uses). Generic semaglutide received approval for Type 2 diabetes management in adults. However, Canadian physicians are legally permitted to prescribe any approved drug for any use they consider medically appropriate — this is called off-label prescribing. It is standard practice, not a grey area. Thousands of Canadian doctors already prescribe brand-name Ozempic off-label for weight loss every month. The same logic applies to generic semaglutide. Your doctor writes a prescription for 'semaglutide injection' and you fill it with the generic. The off-label use is between you and your physician — the pharmacist dispenses whatever the prescription says.
body_sections.key_point: Off-label prescribing is legal and common in Canada. Doctors routinely prescribe semaglutide for weight loss regardless of the approved indication.

body_sections.heading: Who Qualifies for an Off-Label Semaglutide Prescription for Weight Loss?
body_sections.body: There is no fixed national standard for off-label prescribing, but most Canadian physicians follow Canadian clinical obesity guidelines when deciding who to treat. You are likely to qualify for an off-label semaglutide prescription if: your BMI is 30 or higher; your BMI is 27 or higher with at least one weight-related health condition (high blood pressure, sleep apnea, high cholesterol, pre-diabetes, PCOS, or osteoarthritis); you have tried lifestyle changes (diet and exercise) with limited long-term success; and you do not have contraindications such as a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer, multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN 2), or pancreatitis. A family physician or nurse practitioner can write this prescription. Telehealth providers (see below) can also issue an off-label semaglutide prescription after a virtual assessment.
body_sections.key_point: BMI 30+ or BMI 27+ with a weight-related condition is the standard threshold for most off-label semaglutide prescriptions in Canada.

body_sections.heading: Insurance Reality: Provincial Plans Will Not Cover This
body_sections.body: This is the part most people find out the hard way. Provincial drug plans (ODB in Ontario, PharmaCare in BC, NIHB in Alberta, etc.) cover semaglutide only when prescribed for Type 2 diabetes — not for weight loss. This is true for both brand-name Ozempic and generic semaglutide. If you receive an off-label prescription for weight loss and submit it to your provincial plan, it will be rejected. Private insurance through your employer is a mixed picture — some plans cover GLP-1s for weight management with appropriate documentation; others do not. Before starting, call your benefits provider and ask specifically: 'Is semaglutide injection covered for weight management or obesity treatment?' If yes, ask whether prior authorization is required. The realistic out-of-pocket scenario for most Canadians without T2D coverage: $114–150/month for generic semaglutide. This is significantly lower than the $250–500 previously required for Ozempic, making sustained treatment more feasible.
body_sections.key_point: Provincial drug plans cover semaglutide for T2D only. Most Canadians using it for weight loss pay $114–150/month out of pocket with generics.

body_sections.heading: Telehealth Providers That Prescribe Generic Semaglutide for Weight Loss
body_sections.body: Several Canadian telehealth platforms now offer virtual consultations and prescriptions for semaglutide as a weight loss treatment. As of May 2026, providers include: Felix Health (felix.com), which offers a weight loss program that can include semaglutide prescriptions after a physician assessment — branded Ozempic is approximately $271/month through Felix, and they are adding generic options; Hims & Hers Canada (hims.com/ca), which launched an $149/month program in May 2026 that includes the generic semaglutide prescription and medication; Raven Health and Phoenix Health offer similar programs. When using any telehealth provider, be transparent about your weight loss goals, current medications, and medical history. Most require completion of a health questionnaire and a video or async consultation before issuing a prescription. Prescriptions are sent electronically to a pharmacy of your choice or fulfilled directly by the platform.
body_sections.key_point: Telehealth programs like Hims & Hers ($149/mo including Rx) make off-label generic semaglutide accessible without needing to secure a GP appointment.

body_sections.heading: What to Expect: Dosing, Timeline, and Results
body_sections.body: Generic semaglutide for weight loss uses the same dosing protocol as Ozempic: start at 0.25mg once weekly for 4 weeks, increase to 0.5mg, then to 1mg once you're tolerating it well. For weight loss (not diabetes), physicians sometimes titrate higher — this requires brand-name Wegovy (2.4mg) which is not yet available as a generic. Clinical trials of semaglutide 1mg (the generic dose) in people without diabetes showed approximately 8–10% average body weight loss over 40 weeks. Wegovy (2.4mg) showed approximately 15% average weight loss over 68 weeks — meaningfully more, but at significantly higher cost. Most people start noticing reduced appetite within the first 2–4 weeks. Significant weight loss (5%+ of body weight) is typically seen within 12–16 weeks at effective doses. Side effects — nausea, vomiting, constipation, reduced appetite — are most pronounced during the titration phase and typically diminish after 4–8 weeks. Weight regain after stopping semaglutide is common and significant; most physicians recommend treating obesity as a chronic condition requiring long-term management.

body_sections.heading: Generic Semaglutide vs. Wegovy for Weight Loss: Is the Cheaper Option Enough?
body_sections.body: This is the most common question from people coming off Ozempic or considering GLP-1 therapy for the first time. The honest answer: it depends on your goals. Generic semaglutide at 1mg produces meaningful weight loss — roughly 8–10% of body weight in studies. Wegovy at 2.4mg produces more — roughly 15% of body weight. If your goal is modest weight loss (10–20 lbs) or you have a BMI in the 27–32 range, generic semaglutide at 1mg may be sufficient. If your goal is significant weight loss (30+ lbs) or you have a higher BMI, the extra efficacy of Wegovy may be worth the higher cost — approximately $450–600/month for brand-name Wegovy, or waiting for a generic Wegovy equivalent (not expected until 2027 at the earliest). A practical approach many physicians recommend: start with generic semaglutide at 1mg, evaluate your response at 3 months, and only escalate to Wegovy if you're not achieving adequate results. This keeps costs low while preserving the option to step up.

key_takeaways: Generic semaglutide (Apo-Semaglutide, Dr. Reddy's) is approved for Type 2 diabetes — but doctors can legally prescribe it off-label for weight loss.
At $114–150/month, generic semaglutide cuts the cost of GLP-1 weight loss treatment by roughly two-thirds compared to brand-name Ozempic.
Provincial drug plans cover semaglutide for T2D only. Off-label weight loss use is typically paid out of pocket.
BMI 30+ or BMI 27+ with a weight-related health condition is the standard qualification threshold.
Telehealth providers (Hims & Hers, Felix Health, Raven, Phoenix) offer virtual consultations and prescriptions without needing a GP appointment.
Generic semaglutide at 1mg produces ~8–10% body weight loss on average. Wegovy at 2.4mg produces ~15% — no generic Wegovy is expected before 2027.
Weight regain after stopping is common — most physicians recommend treating obesity as a long-term condition.
content.canadian_context: Canada's status as the first G7 country to approve generic semaglutide is particularly significant for weight loss patients, who have historically been excluded from drug plan coverage and forced to pay full price. Obesity Canada estimates over 8 million Canadians live with obesity (BMI 30+), and fewer than 5% have ever been prescribed a GLP-1 medication — primarily due to cost. At $114/month, generic semaglutide is the first GLP-1 drug priced within reach of many Canadians without drug coverage. Provincial drug plans remain slow to add obesity as a covered indication; advocacy groups including Obesity Canada are pushing for formulary changes alongside the generic launch.

faqs.question: Can I use generic semaglutide for weight loss if I don't have diabetes?
faqs.answer: Yes. While the generics are approved for Type 2 diabetes, doctors can legally prescribe any approved drug off-label for other uses. Canadian physicians already prescribe Ozempic off-label for weight loss, and they can do the same with generic semaglutide. You do not need a diabetes diagnosis to receive this prescription.

faqs.question: Will my insurance cover generic semaglutide for weight loss?
faqs.answer: Provincial drug plans (ODB, PharmaCare, etc.) do not cover semaglutide for weight loss — only for Type 2 diabetes. Private employer insurance varies: some plans include obesity treatment with GLP-1 medications, others do not. Call your benefits provider directly and ask about 'semaglutide injection for weight management' to get a clear answer before filling your prescription.

faqs.question: How much does generic semaglutide cost out of pocket for weight loss?
faqs.answer: At retail pharmacies, approximately $114–150/month for a four-week supply. Through telehealth programs like Hims & Hers Canada, an all-in program (consultation + prescription + medication) is available from $149/month. This compares to $250–500/month for brand-name Ozempic out of pocket.

faqs.question: Is generic semaglutide as effective as Ozempic for weight loss?
faqs.answer: Yes — they are the same drug. Health Canada requires generics to demonstrate bioequivalence to the brand-name product. The active ingredient, dose, and absorption profile are identical. You will experience the same weight loss effects, the same side effects, and the same timeline as you would with Ozempic.

faqs.question: How does generic semaglutide compare to Wegovy for weight loss?
faqs.answer: Generic semaglutide is equivalent to Ozempic 1mg. Wegovy uses a higher dose of semaglutide (2.4mg) specifically approved for chronic weight management. In studies, Wegovy produces approximately 15% average body weight loss vs. approximately 8–10% for 1mg semaglutide. Wegovy is more effective but costs significantly more ($450–600/month brand-name, no generic available until at least 2027). For many patients, starting with generic semaglutide at 1mg is a reasonable approach before considering escalation.

faqs.question: How do I get a prescription for generic semaglutide for weight loss?
faqs.answer: You have two main options: (1) See your family doctor or a nurse practitioner and ask for an off-label semaglutide injection prescription for weight management. Bring your BMI history and any related conditions to support the request. (2) Use a telehealth platform like Hims & Hers Canada, Felix Health, or Raven Health — they offer virtual consultations and can issue prescriptions without a GP appointment, typically within 24–48 hours.

faqs.question: Is there a generic version of Wegovy available in Canada?
faqs.answer: No. The 2026 generics (Apo-Semaglutide and Dr. Reddy's) are equivalent to Ozempic 1mg for diabetes. Wegovy requires a different 2.4mg formulation that has its own separate Health Canada approval. No generic Wegovy has been submitted or approved as of May 2026, and analysts do not expect one before 2027 at the earliest.

faqs.question: What's the difference between generic semaglutide and compounded semaglutide?
faqs.answer: Health Canada-approved generic semaglutide (Apo-Semaglutide) has undergone full bioequivalence testing and is made to pharmaceutical standards. Compounded semaglutide — produced by compounding pharmacies — is not Health Canada-approved and has no regulatory oversight for purity, potency, or sterility. Health Canada has issued warnings about compounded semaglutide. With genuine generics now available at $114/month, there is no reason to use compounded products.
